title: Reverse Bits
description: Walk all 32 bits: shift result left, OR in the lowest bit of n, then shift n right. Coerce with `>>> 0` for unsigned result.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: given a 32-bit unsigned integer `n`, return the integer formed by reversing its 32-bit binary representation — bit at position 0 ends up at position 31 and vice versa. A few quick checks:"

• Is it always exactly 32 bits, or could the width vary?
• Should leading zeros be preserved? (Yes — that's why width matters. `0b1` reverses to `0b10000000…000`, all 32 positions.)
• Should I return a number or a string? (Number, in JS — but I need to coerce to unsigned at the end since bit-reversed values often have the high bit set.)
• Could the input arrive as a negative number (sign bit set)? In JS, bitwise ops are signed int32, so values >= 2^31 come in negative. Worth confirming the contract.
sections.why: The 'exactly 32 bits, preserve leading zeros' detail is the single most important clarification — without it, candidates often write a reverse that strips trailing zeros (which become LEADING zeros after reversal) and lose information. The output-as-number-vs-string question pins down the return type and justifies the final `>>> 0` coercion. Asking about signed-vs-unsigned inputs is the JS-specific touch that shows you understand the language's bitwise semantics — the algorithm itself doesn't care, but the I/O interpretation does.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious solution before optimizing.
sections.say:
"The cleanest 'brute force' is the standard 32-iteration shift loop, which IS the canonical solution here — there isn't really a slower correct approach worth comparing to. But a worse alternative is to convert to a binary string with `n.toString(2).padStart(32, '0')`, reverse the string, and `parseInt(reversed, 2)`. That works but allocates a 32-character string, does string reversal, and re-parses — three allocations vs. zero in the bit-loop version.

"Another approach is divide-and-conquer with bit-mask swaps: swap halves, then swap quarters within each half, then eighths, etc. — five operations total instead of 32 iterations. That's actually faster for high-throughput cases but harder to write from memory; the shift-loop is the right answer in an interview because it's correct on the first try."
sections.why: Reverse Bits is one of those problems where the 'brute force' and the 'optimal' are roughly the same — there's no obvious O(n²)-to-O(n) gap. So instead of pretending there's a brute-force-to-optimal narrative, naming the alternatives honestly (string conversion, divide-and-conquer with masks) shows you know the design space. The divide-and-conquer mention is the senior-tier touch — it's the answer to 'can we do better than O(32)?' (yes, O(log 32) = O(5) with parallel bit-swaps), but you'd only use it in performance-critical code, not an interview where correctness on the first try beats raw speed.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to the shift loop?
sections.say:
"The pattern is a two-stream pipeline: bits flow out of `n` from the right (via `n & 1` and `n >>>= 1`) and into `result` from the right (via `result << 1` then OR with the extracted bit). Because `result << 1` shifts the previous contents leftward, the FIRST bit extracted from `n` ends up at the TOP of `result` after 32 iterations — exactly the reversal you want.

"The three load-bearing pieces: (1) `n & 1` reads the lowest bit, (2) `result = (result << 1) | bit` pushes the bit into result's bottom slot, shifting earlier bits leftward, (3) `n >>>= 1` advances n. The unsigned `>>>` matters — plain `>>` would sign-extend the high bit, polluting the loop with 1s if `n` had the sign bit set."
sections.why: Naming the 'two-stream pipeline' framing is the move that makes the algorithm click — bits flow out of one register and into another, with the shift directions doing the reversal automatically. The `>>>` vs `>>` distinction is the JS-specific gotcha that catches careless candidates: with the wrong shift, the high bit of a signed-negative input would smear 1s into the running n, and you'd loop forever (or return wrong results). Verbalizing why `>>>` specifically is the right choice shows you understand JS's signed-int32 bitwise model.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace a couple of inputs — at least one with a single set bit so you can see the bit travel from position 0 to position 31, plus a more complex case that the L3 prompt uses." Three cases — a low-bit-to-high-bit single-set case, the n=0 degenerate, and the canonical LeetCode example.

examples.note: Single bit at position 0 → must end up at position 31. Result is 2^31.
examples.trace:
n = 1 (0b00000000000000000000000000000001), result = 0
i=0:  low = n&1 = 1; result = (0<<1) | 1 = 1; n >>>= 1 → n = 0
i=1:  low = 0;        result = (1<<1) | 0 = 2; n = 0
i=2:  low = 0;        result = (2<<1) | 0 = 4; n = 0
...(29 more iterations, each just shifts result left by 1)...
i=31: low = 0;        result = (2^30 << 1) | 0 = 2^31 = -2147483648 (signed view)
return result >>> 0 = 2147483648 ✓
(The final >>> 0 reinterprets the int32's sign bit as a large unsigned value.)

examples.note: Degenerate — all 32 bits are 0, reversal is still 0.
examples.trace:
n = 0, result = 0
Loop runs 32 times, each iteration: low=0, result stays 0, n stays 0.
return 0 >>> 0 = 0 ✓

n = 43261596 = 0b00000010100101000001111010011100, result = 0

I won't write all 32 steps, but the structure is:
- Each step pulls the lowest bit of the CURRENT n into result's lowest position
- Then shifts n right by 1 (the next-lowest bit becomes the new lowest)
- After 32 iterations, the original bit at position k of n sits at position (31-k) of result

After all 32 iterations:
result (binary) = 0b00111001011110000010100101000000
result (signed int32) = 964176192 (high bit is 0 here, so no >>> 0 surprise)
return 964176192 ✓

sections.why: The first trace is the one to mention out loud — it shows the round-trip behavior most viscerally: a single bit at position 0 ends up at position 31, which means in signed-int32 view the result is NEGATIVE (-2147483648), and the `>>> 0` coercion is what reinterprets it as the correct unsigned value (2147483648). That's the reason `>>> 0` exists in the algorithm — you can't tell from the third trace alone because its high bit happens to be 0. The n=0 degenerate confirms the loop runs in constant 32 iterations regardless of input (no early exit), which is the right answer for 'is your loop dependent on n?'.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• n=0 → all 32 iterations execute with low=0, result stays 0. Return 0. ✓
• n with only the sign bit set (n = 2^31) → reverses to 1. In JS, the input arrives as -2147483648; the algorithm's `n & 1` correctly returns 0 for that, and the bit propagates through to position 31 of n... wait, actually for this input, position 31 of n is set, which after reversal goes to position 0 of result. The `>>>` shift correctly clears the sign bit each step, so the loop terminates cleanly.
• n with high bit set generally → use `>>>` not `>>` for the right shift on n. Plain `>>` would sign-extend, smearing 1s into n's upper bits forever and breaking termination semantics if you used a `while (n !== 0)` style loop (but the fixed 32-iteration `for` saves you from that). Still, `>>>` is correct because we want pure bit shifts, not arithmetic.
• Result with high bit set → the signed-int32 view will look negative; final `>>> 0` reinterprets as unsigned. This is the ONLY reason `>>> 0` is in the algorithm.
• 64-bit / BigInt inputs → algorithm assumes exactly 32 bits. For BigInt you'd loop 64 times (or whatever width) with `n & 1n` and `n >>= 1n` (BigInt `>>` is arithmetic but doesn't sign-extend in the same way), and skip the `>>> 0` coercion since BigInt is sign-agnostic.
• Verifying round-trip — `reverseBits(reverseBits(n)) === n` should hold for any int32 input; that's a cheap sanity test if you have time at the end.
sections.why: The `>>>` vs `>>` distinction is the load-bearing edge case here. It's also the most JS-specific gotcha in all of bit manipulation — most candidates from other languages don't think about it because their language's right shift is unambiguously logical or unambiguously arithmetic. Calling it out explicitly proves you've internalized JS's two-shift-operator model. The `>>> 0` for the final result is the OTHER critical detail: without it, inputs that reverse to a value with the high bit set return a negative number, which fails most test harnesses silently. The round-trip property is the bonus that proves you can validate your own code.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(1) — the loop runs exactly 32 iterations regardless of input. You could call it O(w) where w is the word width (32 here), but for a fixed-width integer type it's a constant.

Space is O(1) — two integers (`n` and `result`), no auxiliary structures.

If you wanted to extend this: the divide-and-conquer version uses 5 mask-swaps to reverse a 32-bit word in O(log 32) = O(5) operations instead of 32. The masks alternate between adjacent-bit swaps (`0x55555555`), 2-bit pair swaps (`0x33333333`), nibble swaps (`0x0F0F0F0F`), byte swaps (`0x00FF00FF`), and the final 16-bit halves swap. It's the technique used in real hardware popcount and bit-reverse instructions. Same correctness, much faster for tight inner loops — but the shift loop is the right interview answer because it's correct on the first try."
sections.why: The O(1) bound is structural (word width is a constant in the language), so the interesting wrap-up content is the divide-and-conquer extension — it's the answer to 'can you do better?'. Naming the specific masks (`0x55555555` for adjacent swap, etc.) proves you've seen the technique, not just heard of it. The trade-off framing — 'shift loop is right in an interview, divide-and-conquer is right in production' — shows you understand WHEN to prefer each, which is the senior-engineer answer. The same masks reappear in popcount (the SWAR/parallel-bits popcount uses the exact same five masks).

walkthrough.intro: Step through the 32-bit reverse loop. The state panel shows `n` and `result` as full 32-bit binary strings so you can watch n's bits flow rightward (consumed by `n & 1`) while result's bits flow leftward (shifted by `<< 1`). Exactly one bit moves per iteration.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — n=${n}`, state: { n: `${n} (${bin(n)})` } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'init result = 0', state: { n: `${n} (${bin(n)})`, result: `0 (${bin(0)})` } };
yield { line: 5, label: `i=${i}: pulled bit ${low} from n's low end → shifted into result's low end`, state: { i, low, n: `${(n >>> 0)} (${bin(n)})`, result: `${(result >>> 0)} (${bin(result)})` } };
yield { line: 10, label: `return result >>> 0 = ${ret} (reinterpret signed int32 as unsigned)`, state: { n: `${(n >>> 0)} (${bin(n)})`, result: `${(result >>> 0)} (${bin(result)})`, returns: ret } };

notes: Use `>>>` (unsigned right shift) on n so the sign bit does not sticky-fill from the left.
JS bitwise ops yield signed 32-bit ints; finish with `>>> 0` to interpret the result as unsigned.
Exactly 32 iterations regardless of n — every bit position is moved into its mirrored slot.

options: It clears any high-bit garbage left over from intermediate shifts
JS bitwise ops return signed 32-bit; >>> 0 reinterprets as unsigned
It truncates the result to exactly 32 bits in case `result << 1` overflowed into a 33rd bit
It coerces the result from a BigInt back to a regular Number

questions.q: Why use `>>>` instead of `>>` on n during the loop?
options: `>>>` is one CPU cycle whereas `>>` is two, making the 32-iteration loop measurably faster
Unsigned shift avoids sign-bit extension so the high bit clears properly
`>>` returns a BigInt for large n; `>>>` keeps the result as a regular Number
`>>>` rounds toward zero while `>>` rounds toward negative infinity — only the former preserves the bit pattern

questions.q: Order of the two operations inside the loop?
options: Shift n right first, then OR its (now-shifted) lowest bit into result
Shift result left and OR n's lowest bit, THEN shift n right
OR n's lowest bit into result FIRST, THEN shift result left so the bit moves to the next slot
Read n's HIGHEST bit (via `n >>> 31`), OR into result, then shift n left
log2(n) — one iteration per bit position of the input
popcount(n) — one iteration per set bit
Math.ceil(log2(n)) + 1 to cover the high bit

blanks.hint: unsigned right shift to advance n

L3.prompt: Write `reverseBits(n)` that reverses the 32 bits of an unsigned integer. Shift result left, OR in `n & 1`, then `n >>>= 1`. Return `result >>> 0`. Log it for 43261596 and 4294967293.
